Item: RBdimmer AC Dimmer 4A 1ch, STANDARD (Z-C/DIM header)
Dim_status: L-W 50x16 and terminal labels (AC-N / AC-L in / AC-L load) from the owner's product photo and listing. H = screw-terminal block + PCB thickness, NOT measured. Price of the Standard variant not yet checked
Note: One per pump. STANDARD variant chosen over DimmerLink: the controller times the triac itself from the module's Z-C output, which gives both phase-angle and whole-cycle burst control, a supply-period reference, and a drive that stops when firing stops. Header GND/VCC/Z-C/DIM. Screw terminals: AC-N (neutral, the zero-cross reference - carries almost no current; the pump's own neutral goes to the neutral bus, not through the module), AC-L in, AC-L load. MOC3021 confirmed random-phase so genuine phase-cut. BT136S triac (SMD D2PAK, 4A) vs a pump current of 0.46A (coffee) and 0.19A (steam) at 253V, the sizing values under an assumed 0.5 power-factor floor (connector-pinouts.md Pumps: running current) - no heatsink needed. BT136 is the NON-isolated-tab type, so the PCB copper under the triac sits at MT2 and is LIVE - clearance matters when mounting. TIMING IS OURS: from the vendor's ESP32 library, DIM is ACTIVE-HIGH (a high level fires the triac, low idles it), the gate pulse is 100us, the minimum delay after zero-cross is 100us, and the Z-C interrupt is on the RISING edge with a 3000us noise gate to reject triac switching spikes. The library is a reference, not this board's specification: Z-C output type (open-collector or push-pull), pulse width and polarity are NOT published - scope them on arrival. One Z-C serves both pumps (use one module's Z-C only; do not tie the two together). Loss of AC-N or of Z-C removes the timing reference, so firmware must stop firing and raise a fault. FUSE: 1-2A slow-blow in each module's AC-L in feed - it protects the 4A triac and the thin pump leads, which the T10A trunk fuse does not. FIT a 10k pull-down DIM-to-GND at the module header (DIM is active-high; first confirm by meter that the board has none) so a floating or disconnected line cannot fire the pump. Keep the logic wiring under 30cm (vendor), twisted Z-C+GND, away from AC runs; ferrite on the cable if dimming is erratic. The vendor page states no isolation figure (read 2026-10-13) - measure it, do not assume it. OPEN: the fitted triac reads BT136S-600E from the board photo. The W suffix denotes snubberless (high-commutation); B/C/D/E are gate-sensitivity grades - so this appears NOT to be a snubberless part. A vibratory pump is strongly inductive and a standard triac can fail to commutate off on one. A '102' (1nF) marking near the triac may be part of a snubber but cannot be confirmed from a photo. VERIFY whether the board fits a triac snubber (MT1-MT2) - a different device from the valve-relay contact snubbers. LIKELY A NON-ISSUE: commutation stress scales with load current and the rated figures are specified at 4A; the pump current is 0.46A, the sizing value under an assumed 0.5 power-factor floor. Do not add a snubber pre-emptively - if insurance is ever wanted the right fix is a snubberless (BTA-xxx-BW) triac.

Item: RC snubber + MOV module (100nF/220R + 10D471K)
Dim_status: L-W confirmed from product photo / H not found
Note: Two needed: one per solenoid valve (the 3-way diverter and the 2-way vent), matching the two snubbed relay channels in module-interconnect.csv; add one per extra valve channel only if a spare channel is ever used. Prebuilt module: 100nF 630V X-class series 220R, in parallel with a 10D471K varistor, on a 2-way screw terminal. 220R is BETTER than the 100R previously specified - it limits the cap discharge surge into closing contacts to 1.5A at 325V peak instead of 3.3A. The 470V varistor is correct HERE (across contacts it must not conduct at normal line peak) even though the mains-inlet MOV is deliberately the lower 275VAC/431 class - different job. NOTE: 100nF is 31.8k at 50Hz, in series with the 220R and the solenoid coil (2.5k measured cold, connector-pinouts.md; |Z| about 31.9k), so about 7.2mA flows with the contacts OPEN, leaving about 18V permanently across the coil taken as its cold resistance (7.2mA x 2.5k, the lower bound) to about 31-51V on the sealed coil (impedance 230^2/VA = 3.92-5.88k from the 9-13.5 VA marking, 7.95-8.63mA), 8-22 % of line; the plunger-open state lies between and is not recorded. Whether that holds a valve in is NOT ESTABLISHED (no drop-out or holding voltage is recorded for the coils, so the residual of up to about 51V, 22 % of line, is neither shown to be too little nor enough; the vent valve's fail-safe state rests on it, to confirm on the bench), and 'de-energised' is no longer zero - relevant to the fail-safe vent hypothesis and to servicing isolation. Not fitted on any generic relay module. DO NOT FIT THESE TO THE PUMP TRIACS. 100nF passes ~7.2mA at 50Hz and a BT136's holding current is only ~10-25mA by grade, so this module risks latching the triac permanently on. A triac snubber, if one is ever needed, is a much smaller RC (about 39R+10nF or 100R+47nF, 0.7-3.4mA) fitted MT1-MT2 - a different device for a different problem.

Item: XDB401 3.3V I2C
Dim_status: thread UNCONFIRMED (G1/4 BSP assumed; the datasheet lists NPT1/8 and NPT1/4; confirm with the seller)
Note: G1/4 BSP is UNCONFIRMED (the sheet lists NPT1/8 and NPT1/4 as standard; confirm with the seller). Same body across ranges and across I2C/analog variants. 1.2MPa brew / 0.5MPa steam. Fixed 0x7F address. DATASHEET (owner-supplied, generic XDB401 family; the 3.3V I2C variant falls under 'others on request', so confirm its output rate and its thread with the seller - the sheet lists NPT1/8 and NPT1/4 as standard): accuracy +/-1% FS (brew 1.2MPa: +/-0.12 bar; steam 0.5MPa: +/-0.05 bar), response time <=4 ms, operating temperature -40 to 105C, compensated range -20 to 80C with drift <=+/-0.03% FS per C, overload 150% FS, burst 300% FS, IP65, 304 stainless, insulation resistance >100 MOhm, long-term stability <=0.2% FS per year, current <=3 mA. CONSEQUENCES: the STEAM tap sits behind a 100-150mm downhill PTFE condensate drop leg with the sensor at the lowest point (D14), so the sensor sees near-ambient water and not steam (saturated steam at 150C and up is far above the 105C limit); a stainless capillary is the fallback. A brew tap AFTER the block sees about 95C, outside the compensated range, adds up to about +/-0.9% FS of extra drift at 95C (about 0.1 bar on the brew sensor), and the 110C coffee thermostat trip is above the 105C limit, so it also needs a capillary. A brew tap BEFORE the block (between the new brew OPV and the block, cold water) sits inside the compensated range and needs none - the chosen placement (D13, Agreed). Steam overpressure check, gauge and absolute labelled: the 0.5MPa part has overload 150% FS = 7.5 bar gauge and burst 300% FS = 15 bar gauge (about 16 bar absolute). If no OPV caps the block, the block is bounded only by the 200C thermostat, so it reaches about 15.5 bar absolute (about 14.5 bar gauge) at the trip and about 17 bar absolute (about 16 bar gauge) at the thermostat tolerance: above the 7.5 bar gauge overload either way, and above the 15 bar gauge burst at the tolerance. So the sensor is not the pressure limit. The steam OPV caps the block only if no check valve lies between it and the block (to be inspected); until that is seen the OPV is not established as the pressure limit for the block (OBL-ELECTRICAL-THERMAL-SAFETY-001.C5). The 4 ms response is about an 85 Hz bandwidth: the 50 Hz pump ripple fundamental passes at roughly 85-90% and harmonics are attenuated. Orient so air can rise back into the main line (sensor below the tee). Keep any capillary bore about 1.5mm so it cannot scale shut. I2C CHIP (INFERRED: the owner's NSA2302 datasheet, NovoSense, matches the all-ones 0x7F address; confirm with the seller that the I2C variant uses it - pages 1-19 and 25-28 of the 32 read): 24-bit sigma-delta ADC, 1 MHz modulator clock, I2C up to 400 kHz, single-shot conversions only (write COMMAND 0x30: sco=1, CMD=001 sensor or 010 temperature plus sensor; poll DRDY at 0x02 bit 0; read PDATA 0x06-0x08, 24-bit signed). The only autonomous mode is 'sleep conversion' with an interval of 62.5 ms to 1 s, so a fast stream means the host triggers each conversion. Output rate is set by OSR_P (EEPROM-backed register 0xA6): 256X to 32768X; the sheet gives no Hz figure, my inference is about 1 MHz divided by OSR (roughly 3.9 kHz at 256X, 1 kHz at 1024X, 30 Hz at 32768X) before per-conversion power-up overhead - measure it. Resolution is not the limit (about 15.8 effective bits at 256X); the element's 4 ms response is. The I2C ADDRESS IS PROGRAMMABLE: register 0xA3 (Chip_Address, Ex_addr_en) in the EEPROM, so two units can be re-addressed to share one bus - an EEPROM write on a calibrated sensor (manual single-register mode via 0x6A/0x6B/0x6C, about 0.8 s, 10k endurance, supply 3-5.5V), best done with the seller. The current plan keeps the two separate buses, which also gives each sensor its own 400 kHz for fast sampling.

Used as an elbow: the block outlet goes into one run port, the branch goes on to the 3-way valve, and the opposite run port carries the probe gland with the probe pointing back into the oncoming flow. The flow turns at the tee, which mixes it (a heated laminar stream is cooler at the core than its mixed average), and the tip faces upstream with the sheath behind it. A Y with an upstream-facing angled probe port is the second choice and a plain T with a cross-flow probe is to be avoided. STEAM tap (REQ-MEASUREMENT-001.C8, DEC-STEAM-PRESSURE-SENSOR-ADDED): in the line between the steam block and the manual steam knob valve (owner statement), upstream of the valve so a closed valve stops milk suck-back reaching the tap, with the drop-leg tube below it; it reads the pressure in the block, not the pump side (a cold-side steam tap adds the unmeasured two-phase block drop). Steam tee rating: saturated steam at the 200C thermostat trip, about 15.5 bar absolute (reference-machine.md); the steam OPV is downstream of the pump's check valve and caps the block at its 4-5 bar setting if no check valve lies between it and the block (to be inspected); until that is seen, size to the steam thermostat trip. If confirmed, size to at least 160C and 8-10 bar (saturated steam at 4-5 bar gauge is about 152-159C). Price is an estimate, not looked up.

Item: Drop-leg tube for the steam pressure tap: PTFE matched to the OEM steam or brew PTFE size and wall (measure OD and ID), 100-150mm per sensor (buy 0.5m); stainless 304/316 capillary 3mm OD x 1.5mm ID, 300mm, as the fallback
Note: A plain drop leg DOWNHILL from the steam tee, no rising section, sensor at the lowest point so air rises back into the steam line. The leg fills with condensate (distilled, no scale): the sensor sees water at near ambient and the pressure is transmitted through the water/steam boundary. Estimated from textbook properties, not measured: heat penetrates a stagnant water column only mm to about 1cm in minutes, so 100-150mm keeps the sensor end cool; check with the spare commissioning chip on the tube next to the sensor (aim under about 60C, the sensor is compensated to 80C). Route it away from the block and other hot parts so the seal does not boil off. About 2ml for 150mm if the bore is 4mm; the OEM tube's bore is not yet measured, and a 4mm OD tube holds less. One leg only: the brew tap has none. PTFE is acceptable only if its pressure rating at the hot-side maximum is confirmed with the supplier: the steam OPV caps the block only if no check valve lies between it and the block (to be inspected) (otherwise the pressure after the block is the saturation pressure at the block temperature, about 15.5 bar absolute at the 200C trip, far less at normal steam temperatures; if it does cap at 4-5 bar gauge, the steam is about 152-159C, so rate to at least 160C and 8-10 bar), the OEM steam line is already PTFE, the OEM tube size and joint method are matched, and the real maximum block temperature is established; if not, use the stainless capillary or 4mm metal tube. Replace the leg at service intervals. Milk suck-back is the contamination risk: tap upstream of the steam valve. The brew tap has no leg (cold side, direct tee). Price is an estimate, not looked up.

Note: One adaptor per sensor. Brew: from the tee's branch thread to the XDB401's G1/4 BSP. Steam: from the drop-leg tube (use the OEM joint method on PTFE; PTFE creeps under ferrules) to G1/4. Price is an estimate, not looked up.

Item: IRM-10-5 carrier board: 3x7cm single-sided copper-clad FR4 blank, M3 standoffs, insulating cover
Dim_status: Estimate. Footprint of the module and its carrier together; price is a lump estimate
Note: REQUIRED on the carrier: nothing beyond the module and its terminals - the IRM-10 needs no external input or output parts and meets EMI Class B on its own (block diagram: EMI filter, rectifiers, switching, output rectifier and filter, opto feedback; Class II, no earth pin, no minimum load stated). RECOMMENDED: the T2A slow-blow fuse in the live (its own line below - no fuse is shown in the diagram or mentioned in the spec sheets read) and the output capacitors (own line below). FR4 is the board material (glass-fibre epoxy); a prototype board is FR4 with copper pads, and a copper-clad blank is FR4 with a solid copper layer. The IRM has four 1.0mm pins that are NOT on a 2.54mm grid (38.5mm between the AC/L-AC/N column and the -V/+V column; 10.75mm AC/L to AC/N; 8mm -V to +V; 3.6mm from the long ends, 3.45mm from the top), so a standard perfboard will not take them. Use a BLANK single-sided copper-clad FR4 board, drill the four pin holes from a 1:1 print of the datasheet footprint, drill the terminal-block and fuse-holder holes, then cut the copper into islands (rotary tool with a thin cutting or diamond wheel, or a hobby knife for scoring; check by meter that each island is isolated). GAP WIDTH MATTERS: between the AC/L and AC/N islands, and between either and anything else on the mains side, remove a band of copper at least 4-5mm wide (and slot the board if you can) - a 1mm cut leaves far too little creepage at 230V; about 1mm is fine only between the 5V +V and -V islands. Buy the blank pre-cut to 3x7cm if possible. FR4 dust is a glass-fibre irritant: P2 mask, eye protection, ideally cut wet or with a vacuum: one island each for AC/L-in with its terminal, AC/L-to-module (the T2A fuse holder bridges the cut between them), AC/N with its terminal, +V with its terminal and the output caps, -V with its terminal and the caps. Mains in at one end and 5V out at the other: the module's own 38.5mm pin separation keeps primary and secondary apart. Use 5.08mm-pitch PCB terminal blocks rated 300V or more for mains in. Mains-side links in insulated mains-rated wire where an island cannot be shared. Insulating cover over the mains terminals; M3 standoffs; keep clear air around the module for convection. A small two-layer custom PCB from a board house would be the cleaner way to do the same job if a custom board is acceptable. ALTERNATIVE FOUND: a community PCB for 5-10W and 15-20W IRM modules with room for an output filter (theslowdiyer.wordpress.com/2021/04/15/project-files-irm-psus-from-a-different-angle/, Gerbers provided, Eagle, licence not stated, no creepage figures given, board dimensions and pin match to the IRM-10 not verified). The module is mounted rotated 90 degrees, which would stand it on its 25.4mm edge: check that height plus board against the usable height (28mm elsewhere and 23.4mm within about 2mm of a wall) before relying on it

Item: Conformal coating spray, acrylic and Kapton (polyimide) masking tape, 10mm x 33m roll [RECOMMENDED]
Note: For the IRM carrier (hand-cut copper, exposed islands, mains on one side) and, optionally, the perfboard. Recommended because humidity inside the enclosure is declared as condensing (the worst case until measured; see reference-machine.md § Ambient) and the interior sees thermal cycling, and a coat guards the cut copper against corrosion and tracking across the gaps. IT DOES NOT REPLACE CREEPAGE: the 4-5mm gaps and the module's own 38.5mm pin separation must stand on their own. Apply after the meter checks and a powered test; mask the terminal screws, the fuse holder contacts and anything that gets reworked. Acrylic is rated well above the 70C worst case and can be soldered through if a joint needs rework; do not coat the IRM's printed label. The insulating cover over the mains terminals is a separate, touch-protection job. Price is an estimate. QUANTITY: the boards total about 0.017 m2 even coated on both sides (carrier 70x30mm, perfboard 70x90mm); at a 25-75um film that is only a few ml of liquid, so buy the smallest size - a 30ml brush-on bottle (easier to mask and control) or the smallest aerosol, about 100-200ml, which will be mostly left over. Kapton tape for the masking: it is solvent-resistant, leaves no residue and survives soldering heat. It is for masking only - do not use tape as the mains insulation barrier

Note: Paste, not putty. Under the NTC plug face a thin bond line gives the fastest and least offset reading; putty is a thicker gap filler with higher thermal resistance and is slower. Must be rated at or above the block temperature (the steam block's thermostat trips at 200C) and must be NON-CONDUCTIVE: the thermistor element sits exposed in a slot in the plug face, so a metal-filled or liquid-metal compound can bridge its leads or short it to the block - and gallium-based liquid metal attacks aluminium. Clean old compound off with isopropyl alcohol, apply a rice-grain amount, press flat, wipe excess. Price is an estimate

Item: ULN2003A 7-channel driver breakout board (SSR drive)
Dim_status: NOT MEASURED. Footprint area is an ESTIMATE (about 50x28mm) from the owner's listing photo. Price is an estimate
Note: Buy 2: 1 fitted, 1 spare. One board covers both heaters (2 of 7 channels, IN1/IN2 to PB0/PB1; the other five unused). It sinks each SSR's control input from the 5V rail: the SSR needs 7.5-12mA at 3-32VDC and a 3V3 GPIO cannot supply that reliably. The 24mA in the mA column is the two SSR control currents (2 x up to 12mA) drawn from the 5V rail, not a GPIO current; the 5V budget carries 29mA for it (see module-interconnect.csv). The Darlington drops about 1V, so each SSR sees about 4V - above its 3V minimum, but measure it. Lives in the control cavity next to the controller; only the two 5V SSR control pairs go down to the SSRs in the bottom zone. SAFETY: a floating or reset GPIO must leave the heater OFF (OBL-ELECTRICAL-THERMAL-SAFETY-001.C2). The chip's inputs should default off through internal resistors, but that is a datasheet claim not yet confirmed on this breakout, so KEEP an external 10k pull-down across each used input and GND, fitted at the breakout board's own header pins so it still holds if the controller cable comes off, until the board has been measured. Unknown on the board: the GND/VCC jumper header's function and whether the D1-D4 LEDs load the outputs. Check the chip marking (fakes). Replaces the earlier 2x logic-level FET design

Item: PT1000 thin-film flat chip, Class A claimed, welded leads, rated 250C or more (temporary puck-inlet probe at commissioning, plus spare)
Dim_status: Chip size from the listing photo; price is an estimate
Note: NOT fitted to the blocks any more: the block NTCs stay as casing sensors (see temperature-sensing-front-end.md). One chip is the TEMPORARY probe at the puck inlet (in a dummy puck or the basket path) for the commissioning identification runs; one is a spare because chips and their fine leads are fragile. BEFORE TRUSTING A CLASS A CLAIM from a marketplace seller: it is a label, not a test. Sanity check: about 1090 ohm at room temperature (a PT100 reads about 109, an NTC reads wildly differently); ice point (stirred ice slush) and boiling point on the whole measurement chain; then heat-cycle and re-check the ice point. Check the listing rates leads and chip joint at 250C: tin-lead solder melts at 183C and lead-free creeps near 217C, so welded leads are what you want. Price is an estimate, not looked up.

Item: Resistor 4.7k LOW-TCR (25ppm/C or better) metal film, through-hole
Note: Need 6: the sensor dividers - 3 for the PT1000s (the outlet water probe, the temporary puck-inlet probe and the steam-output monitor) (4.7k keeps the chip current near 0.5mA and self-heating near 0.4mW; a 1k reference would push about 1.4mA and 2.6mW into the chip) and 3 for the NTCs (wand disc plus the two block NTCs kept as a plausibility check). Specify by TCR, not initial tolerance: three-point Steinhart-Hart calibration absorbs initial tolerance but not drift. A generic 100-pack is usually 50-100ppm/C and does not meet this.
